name: Cosmos
lede: Cosmos is a light reddish purple from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, named for the garden flower, and rare in painting.

sections.title: A name in an old dictionary
sections.body:
Cosmos appears as a color name in Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930, on plate 50, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 later folded the shade into its block called light reddish purple, about 2.8 units from this swatch [1]. The books in our collection do not say why the authors chose the name, so its origin is undocumented here [1][2].

The plain reading is the flower. Cosmos is a garden plant in the daisy family, and one species, *Cosmos sulphureus*, was the base of an organic colorant used to illuminate manuscripts in Mesoamerica [3]. That dye is yellow-orange, not this pink-mauve, so the flower and the swatch share a name more than a color [3][1].

sections.title: The plant and its light
sections.body:
Cosmos is a short-day plant, meaning it flowers when the days shorten, and Birren cites it with salvia as one that red light hindered in experiments [4]. That is a fact about how plants read light, not about the color of the petals [4].

The word has other meanings in the books: the cosmos of the sun in late antique religion [5], and the early Christian preference for dark blue-violets to suggest the cosmos or divinity [6]. None of these concerns this swatch, so we do not link it to them [5][6].

sections.title: Near neighbors
sections.body: This swatch sits among the pink-purples. It is lighter and warmer than [[orchid]] and less blue than [[lilac]], with [[mauve]] on the grey side [1]. The ISCC-NBS name for the block, light reddish purple, is the plain description [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 9 works, or 0.04 per cent, rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors [7]. Only five paintings hold it on at least 5 per cent of the canvas: Matisse's *The Roofs of Collioure* and *Portrait of Madame Matisse (The Green Line)*, Kirchner's *Two Girls under an Umbrella* of 1910, Gauguin's *Fatata te Miti* of 1892 and an Indian goddess painting of about 1900 [7]. All five date from 1892 to 1910 [7].

So in our archive cosmos pink turns up in early modern work, from 1892 to 1910 [7]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [7].

origin.named_after: origin undocumented in our sources; likely the flower
